source.title: On the Role of Optimization in Double Descent: A Least Squares Study
source.authors: Ilja Kuzborskij; Csaba Szepesvari; Omar Rivasplata; Amal Rannen-Triki; Razvan Pascanu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error while varying network width on MNIST and FashionMNIST, and analyzes double descent in least-squares gradient descent. These are conceptual tests rather than a stated replication of the original study's full method and settings.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites double-descent results from prior work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. The reported outcomes of the paper's own least-squares analysis and neural-network experiments are included.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-error-vs-width sweeps in MLPs on MNIST/FashionMNIST, plus a synthetic noiseless linear-regression excess-risk curve (Fig. 1). It offers an optimization-based account, the smallest positive feature eigenvalue, of where and why the peak occurs. This is a different method aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors find noiseless double descent in least squares is explained solely by optimization, via the smallest positive eigenvalue that follows the Bai-Yin law. Label noise additionally enlarges the peak. For neural networks they show depth and width affect this eigenvalue differently and present the link as a conjecture.
record.recipe_differences: The paper derives bounds for gradient descent on least squares and empirically studies one- and three-hidden-layer MLPs on MNIST and FashionMNIST; it is not presented as a reproduction of the original study's full settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error increase and minimum-eigenvalue behavior vary with architecture, including depth and bottleneck structure. The width experiments also show results at multiple training-update snapshots.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed width 500, deeper MLPs reach higher test error and smaller last-layer minimum eigenvalues under plain GD. The 10-layer net fails to train well within 10000 iterations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature ill-conditioning from depth degrades GD test error independently of the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Skip connections make a 3-layer net's penultimate-layer minimum eigenvalue at initialization behave like a 1-layer net's. The condition number follows the minimum eigenvalue while the maximum stays between 10 and 100 (App. B, G.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural choices such as skip connections reduce the eigenvalue drop at the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: The neural-network experiments use 1000 training examples. The text says the MNIST Figure 2 behavior is consistent under 5 random seeds, while other test-error error bars are estimated by splitting the test set into 10 subsets. Several numerical results are presented only in figures. The empirical neural-network evidence is limited to small MLPs and two image datasets; the proposed eigenvalue account for neural networks is described as a conjecture.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row was created for every plotted training-update snapshot, learning-rate curve, or individual depth/width point; the text-level findings and stated comparisons are recorded instead. Exact values for those plot traces are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Only small MLPs (1 and 3 hidden layers), 1000 training examples, MNIST/FashionMNIST; no CNNs/ResNets/transformers or label-noise settings.
Not tested: only three iteration snapshots are shown, with no test-error curve over training time.
Only GD on least squares (theory plus a synthetic n=20 example); no other model classes such as random features, trees or kernels.
Peak location along epochs or sample count is not tested; only the width axis.
No empirical label-noise sweep, no multiple peaks, no test of whether optimal regularization removes the peak.

missing.what: Synthetic linear regression (n=20, d in [100], GD α=0.05, noise-free labels): estimated excess risk on held-out points and the optimization-error term both peak as d varies.
Explicit statement that in noiseless regression DD is explained solely by optimization quantities.

record.verdict_notes: The peak in the MLP sweeps occurs at hidden width ≈ number of training samples (1000), not at a parameter count. Most numbers appear only in figures. The theoretical results are upper bounds, so the theory rows alone cannot establish curve shapes.

versions.untested_parts: The neural-network experiments vary width in small MLPs, not a broad range of deep-network architectures or model families.
No test-error curve over training time at fixed model size is reported.
The paper does not report a test-error sweep in which training-sample count increases near the interpolation threshold.
The theoretical result is for least-squares gradient descent; the empirical neural-network tests cover small MLPs on two image datasets, not a broad set of model classes.

The proposed minimum-positive-eigenvalue account is explored for width and architecture. It is not tested as a predictor across epochs or sample size, nor established as a single effective-complexity measure.
The analysis gives a theoretical label-noise dependence. The paper does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not replot the second descent against an effective parameter count to assess whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: gradient descent solution of least-squares regression
rows.size_stated: feature dimension d; overparameterized regime d > n
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the excess-risk bound as feature dimension d varies at fixed n and T.
rows.measure: Theorem 2 excess-risk upper bound; its data-dependent factor is described as having double-descent behavior as d varies.
rows.value: The bound contains the factor (1 − αλ̂⁺min)²T; the paper states that this factor has double-descent behavior as model size d varies.
rows.note: This is a theoretical bound, not a numerical measurement of test risk. The bound also contains another term, and the paper says that term can be negligible in many cases.
rows.check: An upper bound on excess risk cannot show the shape of the risk itself. The double-descent shape is argued for one factor of the bound, not measured. The empirical counterpart is Fig. 1, which has no row (see missing).

rows.subject: gradient descent solution of least-squares regression
rows.size_stated: feature dimension d; overparameterized regime d > n
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the noisy-regression excess-risk bound and its dependence on label-noise variance.

conditions.value: noise with mean zero and variance σ²

rows.measure: Theorem 3 excess-risk upper bound and stated effect of noise on the peak.
rows.value: The bound adds (4σ²/n) E[(λ̂⁺min)⁻²]; the authors state that more noise is expected to make the peak larger.
rows.note: The noise dependence is an analytical result and interpretation of a bound, not an empirical noise-level sweep.
rows.check: The noise term is an added term in an upper bound. 'Larger peak with more noise' is the authors' expectation, not a measured noise sweep. 'Observed' overstates it.

rows.subject: three-hidden-layer MLP on MNIST, with all hidden layers widened
rows.size_stated: width increased in all hidden layers
rows.operation_detail: Increase hidden-layer widths and measure test error and the minimum positive eigenvalue of the last hidden-layer features.
rows.measure: Test error and minimum positive eigenvalue of last-layer features.
rows.value: The authors report a drop in the minimum eigenvalue when the last hidden layer reaches the training-sample count; the deeper network has a larger eigenvalue drop and a higher test-error increase around the interpolation threshold.
rows.uncertainty: For experiments other than the MNIST Figure 2 experiment, test-error mean and standard errors are estimated by splitting the test set into 10 subsets.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison qualitatively; exact values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: For V1, the 3-layer width sweep shows a larger test-error rise near the threshold. For V5, the eigenvalue drop occurs when last-layer width reaches n, and its magnitude depends on earlier layers.

rows.subject: three-hidden-layer MLP on MNIST, with a bottleneck in earlier layers
rows.size_stated: last hidden layer widened; earlier hidden layers kept at a fixed small size
rows.operation_detail: Increase the last hidden-layer width while earlier layers form a bottleneck; measure test error and feature eigenvalue.
rows.measure: Test error and minimum positive eigenvalue of last-layer features.
rows.baseline: three-hidden-layer network with all hidden layers widened
rows.value: The paper reports a more pronounced eigenvalue drop around width 1000 for the bottleneck network; its eigenvalue remains smaller at larger widths and this is reflected in higher test error.
rows.uncertainty: For experiments other than the MNIST Figure 2 experiment, test-error mean and standard errors are estimated by splitting the test set into 10 subsets.
rows.locator: Appendix F, Figure 7 and accompanying text
rows.note: This comparison shows that architecture affects the measured eigenvalue and error; it does not establish that the eigenvalue alone predicts peak location.
rows.check: The text reports a sharper eigenvalue drop at last-layer width 1000 and higher test error overall. It does not describe the bottleneck test-error curve as double descent, so the V1 link is unsupported. The eigenvalue locates the drop, but its size depends on architecture.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5: the bottleneck produces a sharper eigenvalue dip near last-hidden-layer width 1000 and higher test error, but the text does not identify a bottleneck test-error peak whose location the eigenvalue predicts.

source_check.problem: Architectural dependence of eigenvalue magnitude and error does not establish a partial failure of V5's peak-location prediction.

rows.subject: MLP family on MNIST with hidden width 500
rows.size_stated: hidden width 500; depth varied from 2 to 10
rows.operation_detail: Increase network depth and measure test error and the minimum eigenvalue of last-layer features.
rows.measure: Test error and minimum eigenvalue of last-layer features.
rows.value: The authors report that deeper networks have higher test error and smaller minimum eigenvalues; the deepest network does not obtain reasonable performance even after 10000 iterations.
rows.uncertainty: Test-error means and standard errors are estimated by splitting the test set into 10 subsets.
rows.locator: Appendix F, Figure 6 and accompanying text
rows.note: This is a depth sweep, not a width sweep across an interpolation threshold; it shows worsening test error with increasing depth in this setting.
rows.check: This is a fixed-width (500 < n = 1000) depth sweep that never crosses the interpolation threshold. Rising error with depth is an optimization-difficulty result, not a reversal of model-wise double descent. 'Reversed' is wrong; the row belongs under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: 1- and 3-hidden-layer MLPs, width sweep, 1000 MNIST/FashionMNIST training examples, plain GD
relationships.reason: Test error peaks near 1000 hidden units (= n) and then falls again (R3, R4, R7). The peak is small in the 1-layer nets and larger in the 3-layer net.
relationships.display_finding: Test error peaked near 1000 hidden units and then decreased; the peak was smaller with one hidden layer than with three.

relationships.reason: The minimum positive eigenvalue of hidden features dips exactly where test error peaks (width = n), and this persists through training (R5, R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: The minimum positive feature eigenvalue dipped exactly at the test-error peak, where width equaled n, throughout training.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R5–R7 associate the minimum-positive feature-covariance eigenvalue dip with the width-axis test-error peak. Support is restricted to this association; prediction across epochs or sample counts is untested.

relationships.condition: 3-hidden-layer nets with bottleneck vs wide earlier layers
relationships.reason: The drop location tracks last-layer width, not total size. Drop magnitude and error depend on earlier layers, so size alone does not set the quantity (R7, R8). The authors call the neural-network link a conjecture.
relationships.display_finding: The spectral drop followed last-layer width, while earlier layers affected its magnitude and test error; the authors described the neural-network connection as conjectural.

source_check.condition: 3-hidden-layer nets with bottleneck vs wide earlier layers
source_check.reason: R7–R8 show that raw size does not determine feature conditioning. They do not show that the proposed spectral measure fails to locate a peak; R8 does not establish a bottleneck test-error peak. Conjectural status alone does not justify limits_scope.

relationships.condition: noiseless least squares trained by GD for finite T
relationships.reason: Per the text (Fig. 1 and the abstract, no row), the peak appears with no label noise. The authors attribute noiseless DD solely to optimization; noise only enlarges the peak, per the R2 bound.
relationships.display_finding: A peak appeared without label noise and was attributed solely to optimization, while added noise enlarged it.
